text: Every staking or farming reward comes from somewhere — usually a fixed pool of tokens set aside at launch, paid out according to a schedule written into the contract. Two shapes dominate: linear emission and decaying emission.

Linear emission releases the same number of tokens every block, for as long as the reserve lasts. At 10 tokens per block and 2 million blocks a year, that's 20 million tokens a year — a 100 million token reserve lasts exactly 5 years, then emissions stop entirely.

Decaying emission shrinks the rate on a schedule, most commonly by halving at fixed intervals, the Bitcoin pattern. Starting at 50 tokens per block and halving every 210,000 blocks, the rate drops to 25, then 12.5, approaching but never quite reaching zero — front-loading early adopters.

A linear schedule with no end in sight can make farmers treat the yield as permanent income rather than a bootstrap subsidy. A decaying schedule explicitly tells participants emissions are richest now and will shrink — which is exactly what triggers farm and dump: maximize the current rate, sell immediately, move to the next opportunity before the halving.

Protocols trying to avoid both failure modes combine three moves: bootstrap high to attract initial liquidity, taper on a schedule announced in advance so participants can plan around it, and shift weight toward real yield as fee revenue grows, so emissions aren't the permanent engine.

A protocol might go from 90% emissions and 10% real fees in year one, to 20% emissions and 80% real fees by year three. Next: token supply models, and the design decisions that determine how big that emission reserve even is.
